title: Production and safety
why: The questions that separate juniors: what happens when it fails, costs too much or gets attacked? Answering those well is what moves you to mid-level bands.
outcomes: Recognise and defend against prompt injection
Keep personal data out of logs
Cut cost with caching, routing and shorter context
Set and measure a latency budget
lessons: Read the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications and map each risk to your projects
Try to prompt-inject your own RAG app; fix what breaks
Redact personal data before logging; set retention
Cut cost: cache repeats, route easy questions to a smaller model, trim context
Set a p95 latency budget and measure against it
resources: Optional, about £45; the best single book on the field
method: Attack your own work. A short 'what I broke and how I fixed it' section in each README is strong interview material.
build: A SECURITY.md and a cost and latency table added to projects 1 and 3.

o: Untrusted content containing instructions that hijack the model
quiz.e: Retrieved pages, emails or user text can carry instructions; the model may follow them.

o: Treat retrieved text as data, give tools least privilege, require approval for risky actions
quiz.e: Limit what a hijacked model can do; don't rely on it never being hijacked.

quiz.q: A good way to reduce cost:
o: Cache repeats and route simple queries to a smaller model
quiz.e: Most traffic is easy; route it cheaply.

o: 95% of requests finish within this time
quiz.e: Percentiles show the tail users actually feel; averages hide it.

quiz.q: Personal data in logs should be:
o: Redacted before logging, with a retention period
quiz.e: Logs leak. Don't store what you don't need.
